A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work and their supplied pages are readable. v1 includes Appendices A–G, but v2 ends with references on page 11 despite citing unavailable appendices, including A–D and H–J. The main texts support comparison, while appendix-dependent judgments remain limited.

before.justification: v1 reports original speech-extraction experiments, baseline comparisons, ablations, robustness analyses, and successful and failed examples in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark results, training and fusion ablations, interferer-duration experiments, and a study using ten users' enrollment labels.

M1.justification: The stated enrollment-embedding pooling kernel changes from 20 in v1 Section 3.2 to 40 in v2 Section 3.3. The shared TF-GridNet encoders, segmentation embeddings, attention fusion, causal extraction branch, and two-stage losses otherwise match. The Siamese Encoder terminology does not establish a new component.

E1.justification: LibriSpeech and WHAM remain, while binaural impulse-response sources expand from ASH-Listening-Set to include CIPIC, RRBRIR, and CATTRIR. v2 also evaluates partial temporal overlap with positive-only interferers and inaccurate human enrollment labels, materially extending the input conditions examined in v1. Coverage claimed only in v2's missing appendices cannot be verified.

E2.justification: The visible main comparisons retain TCE, SpeakerBeam, NMF, LookOnceToHear, and the FiLM variant; ADEnet is discussed but not evaluated there. However, v2 defers a clean-enrollment comparison to unavailable Appendix J, preventing verification of comparator membership across all experiments.

E3.justification: The main evaluation increases from 2000 to 5000 generated test samples and adds STOI and DNSMOS. v2 separately varies enrollment and extraction speaker counts. Its new protocols include controlled interferer-duration sweeps over 2000 samples and ten users labeling ten simulated mixtures. These substantially revise the evaluation design.

E4.justification: Both versions retain training-stage and fusion ablations. v2 adds controlled tests of positive and negative interferer speech duration (Figures 4–5) and robustness to user labeling errors (Figure 6). These test disambiguation and annotation tolerance beyond v1's whole-enrollment-length analysis. Changes to analyses deferred to missing appendices remain unresolved.

E5.justification: Both versions already report means and standard deviations across evaluation samples. v2 adds an explicit normality assumption, two-sample t-tests at the 90% confidence level for binaural comparisons, and boxplots of variability across users' labels. These extend statistical reporting without establishing additional independent training runs.

E6.justification: v1 Table 2's benchmark results are replaced in the main text by v2 Table 1's revised condition matrix and additional metrics. The convergence finding changes from reaching 5 dB SNR in 520k versus 240k steps to reaching 3 dB in 600k versus 240k steps. New duration and labeling experiments add substantial findings. Changed conditions preclude interpreting these as same-setting performance gains or losses.

T1.justification: v1 defines targets through the speaker-set difference SP minus SN. v2 introduces an explicit nonsynchronous-speaking assumption and distinguishes negative, positive, hybrid, and neglect-required interferers using temporal activity. A speaker present only during part of the positive enrollment can now be an interferer, substantively changing the formal disambiguation framework.

C1.justification: v1 presents a new noisy-enrollment extraction task and highlights multi-target extraction and enrollment-length flexibility. v2 reframes the contribution around temporal speaking patterns, substantial overlap, and imprecise enrollment labels, replacing those highlighted application claims with labeling robustness. It also withdraws the broad claim of being the first monaural method requiring no clean enrollment.

C2.justification: v2 explains how comparisons among positive frames and against negative frames suppress different interferers, and expands the explanation for two-stage training. Section 5 adds a possible frozen-teacher performance ceiling and audible artifacts limiting downstream recognition. These substantially extend v1's interpretations concerning speaker counts, binaural difficulty, input quality, and individual failure cases.

D1.justification: v1 Appendices A–B document preprocessing, STFT settings, parameter counts, optimization budgets, and baseline fine-tuning. v2 delegates corresponding information to unavailable Appendices B–C. Although some settings remain visible in its main text, the supplied material cannot establish which detailed reproducibility information was retained or revised.

R1.justification: v2 newly acknowledges ADEnet as closely related activity-label-driven extraction and differentiates its contribution through high overlap and optimization challenges. This materially revises v1's first-without-clean-enrollment positioning. VoiceFilter and additional impulse-response dataset references also enter the discussion and bibliography.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, problem formulation, architecture explanation, and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting. Related work is condensed from three subsections to two, a speaker-disambiguation subsection is introduced, and ablation discussions are reordered. Terminology changes include disturbing speakers becoming interferers and renamed encoder and fusion components.

P2.justification: The main layout changes from two columns to one. The opening illustration is redrawn around waveform timing, v1 Figures 3–4 are consolidated into v2 Figure 2, and the main results table gains nested experimental conditions and additional metric rows. New duration plots and a user-labeling boxplot substantially change the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v2 Figures 4–6 add useful evidence about disambiguation and labeling tolerance, while its revised positioning and Section 5 limitations improve qualification of the claims. However, the missing cited appendices prevent checking promised assumption validation, clean-enrollment comparisons, reproducibility details, and retention of v1's extensive supplementary analyses. These evidence gaps prevent a reliable assessment of the overall quality balance.
